title: SLEPCIK v. THE NETHERLANDS AND THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary:
In the case of Slepčík v. the Netherlands and the Czech Republic, the applicants were a Roma family from Pardubice, Czech Republic, consisting of a husband, wife, and their four children. As members of the Roma and Travellers community, they alleged that they faced persecution by skinheads in the Czech Republic and that the authorities there failed to protect them, prompting their repeated asylum applications in the Netherlands. The core vulnerability at issue was the risk of racially motivated violence and the lack of effective state protection for Roma, compounded by difficulties in acquiring citizenship following the dissolution of Czechoslovakia.

The family first sought asylum in the Netherlands in August 1992, citing attacks and threats in their hometown. After their initial request was rejected and subsequently withdrawn, they returned to the Netherlands in May 1993 to reapply, but were again refused. Their legal efforts included appeals and interim measures, but Dutch courts ultimately found their claims insufficiently substantiated, noting some police action in response to the attacks in Pardubice and ongoing citizenship proceedings in the Czech Republic.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but found the application inadmissible. The Commission held that asylum and residence proceedings did not fall within the scope of Article 6, and that the applicants had not shown a real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment if returned. No remedies were awarded.

This case highlights the persistent barriers Roma and Travellers face in securing protection from racial violence and statelessness in Europe, reflecting the broader historical context of exclusion and legal uncertainty following the breakup of Czechoslovakia in the 1990s.
